analysis.one_liner: Ends health insurers' exemption from federal antitrust laws against price fixing.
analysis.headline: The bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in a House Judiciary subcommittee in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1945, a federal law called the McCarran-Ferguson Act has let insurance companies escape federal antitrust rules — the laws that make price fixing, bid rigging, and dividing up markets among competitors illegal. This bill would take that protection away from health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, making them play by the same antitrust rules as most other businesses.
analysis.who_benefits: People and employers who buy health insurance, who could benefit from more competition among insurers and potentially lower premiums. The bill would also give the Justice Department and FTC clear authority to prosecute insurers that fix prices or divide up markets, and it would let insurers be sued for anticompetitive conduct just like other companies.

how_it_helps.text: Strips health insurers and medical malpractice insurers of their special protection under the McCarran-Ferguson Act, so they can no longer legally fix prices, rig bids, or divide up markets.
Restores full application of the federal antitrust laws to the business of health insurance, including FTC enforcement against unfair methods of competition even for nonprofit insurers.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and medical malpractice insurers, who would lose a decades-old exemption from antitrust prosecution and face potential lawsuits and enforcement actions for anticompetitive behavior. Some of that cost could be passed through to customers, and the insurers' mutual data-sharing arrangements (like sharing what rates they plan to file with state regulators) could become legally riskier.

drawbacks.text: Removing the exemption might not lower premiums much: insurers say the exemption mainly lets them share data and file proposed rates with state regulators, which can help small insurers compete, and dominant insurers can exercise market power through legal conduct antitrust law does not reach.
The bill does not itself break up or regulate concentrated insurance markets — it only removes a legal shield, so its practical effect on premiums is uncertain and untested.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, targeted fix: it removes one industry's special carve-out from laws everyone else must obey, at essentially no cost to taxpayers. The honest caveat is that it is a tool, not a guarantee — it restores the ability to sue and prosecute, but whether that produces lower premiums depends on how much actual price fixing occurs and how aggressively the laws are enforced. The strongest objection, from the industry, is that data-sharing among insurers has some legitimate uses; the bill's answer is that price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation are not legitimate and should be illegal for insurers as for everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then passed to a subcommittee, and sat there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. John Conyers introduced the bill on January 6, 2015, the opening day of the 114th Congress.

It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee that same day, and on February 2, 2015 was referred to its Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action it ever received.
No cosponsors signed on, no hearing was held, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers are better off: they kept their exemption from antitrust laws against price fixing, bid rigging, and market allocation without ever facing a vote. Consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept their antitrust exemption

for.name: Rep. John Conyers
for.role: Sponsor; Ranking Member, House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the Congress and pressed for it as the committee's top Democrat, but it never advanced past a subcommittee referral.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law and never scheduled a markup or floor vote during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.role: Insurers protected by the McCarran-Ferguson exemption
against.what_they_did: Have long opposed repealing the health insurance antitrust exemption, which shields their rate-filing and data-sharing practices from antitrust suits.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and not a single member of either party signed on as a cosponsor, so the partisan shape of the issue was never tested on this bill — though a similar version passed the Democratic-controlled House in 2010.

industries.note: They would lose their exemption from federal antitrust laws, exposing price fixing, bid rigging, and market division to prosecution and private suits. Because their exemption shields practices that can inflate premiums, their interest runs against insurance customers here.

The bill covers malpractice insurers too, ending their ability to coordinate on pricing without antitrust exposure. Consumers buying coverage in these markets would gain the protection of competition law.
